title: Dangerous Animals of Queensland
subtitle: Lethal, dangerous or harmless? Beyond the snakes
intro: Real photos from iNaturalist observers in Queensland. Decide how dangerous each animal is, then name it.
fieldRule: Field rule: from October to May, wear a stinger suit in tropical Queensland waters and treat every jellyfish as dangerous.

answers.Dangerous: Injury, envenomation or illness, rarely fatal

species.name: Crocodylus porosus
species.note: Broad, heavy snout with no row of large scales behind the head. Lives in rivers, estuaries and the sea, and has killed many people in north Queensland.

species.name: Carcharhinus leucas
species.note: Stocky grey shark with a short, blunt snout and small eyes. Swims far up rivers and canals, including the Brisbane River and Gold Coast waterways.

species.name: Galeocerdo cuvier
species.note: Wide, square snout; dark vertical bars on the back, strongest in young sharks. Responsible for many fatal attacks in Queensland waters.

species.name: Carcharodon carcharias
species.note: Torpedo-shaped, grey above and white below, with a conical snout and black eyes. Mostly south-east Queensland waters.

species.name: Casuarius casuarius
species.note: Tall, black-plumaged bird with a blue neck, red wattles and a horny casque. The inner toe has a dagger-like claw. Killed a teenager near Mossman in 1926.

species.name: Canis dingo
species.note: Ginger to sandy dog with white feet and tail tip and upright ears. A boy was killed on K'gari (Fraser Island) in 2001.

species.name: Chironex fleckeri
species.note: Pale, cube-shaped bell up to 30 cm with bunches of tentacles at each corner. Nearly invisible in water. Can stop the heart within minutes. Coastal north Queensland, October to May.

species.name: Carukia barnesi
species.note: Tiny transparent box jelly, about 2 cm, with four long tentacles. The sting is mild at first; Irukandji syndrome follows 20 to 40 minutes later.

species.name: Malo kingi
species.note: Small box jelly with four tentacles. Named after Robert King, who died after a sting off Port Douglas in 2002.

species.name: Hapalochlaena fasciata
species.note: Small octopus with blue lines (not rings) that glow when it is alarmed. Bite is often painless; tetrodotoxin causes paralysis. There is no antivenom.

species.name: Hapalochlaena lunulata
species.note: Golf-ball-sized octopus with large blue rings that flash when threatened. Rock pools and reef flats. There is no antivenom.

species.name: Conus geographus
species.note: Thin, cone-shaped shell with brown map-like patches. Fires a venomous harpoon. A man died after picking one up on Hayman Island in 1935.

species.name: Conus textile
species.note: Cone-shaped shell covered in a tent-like pattern of brown and white triangles. Same harpoon and venom as the geographic cone.

species.name: Hadronyche infensa
species.note: Glossy black spider with large fangs that point straight down. Rears up when threatened. Burrows in south-east Queensland.

species.name: Hadronyche formidabilis
species.note: Large glossy black funnel-web that lives in tree holes and rotting logs. Capable of severe, potentially fatal envenomation.

species.name: Tetractenos hamiltoni
species.note: Small puffer with a pale belly and brown spots that inflates when caught. Deadly if eaten: its flesh holds tetrodotoxin.

species.name: Pteropus alecto
species.note: Large fruit bat with a black body and reddish collar. Can carry Australian bat lyssavirus and Hendra virus, both of which have killed people in Queensland. Never handle a bat unless vaccinated.

species.name: Aedes aegypti
species.note: Small black mosquito with white bands on the legs and a white lyre pattern on the thorax. Spreads dengue in Far North Queensland.

species.name: Culex annulirostris
species.note: Brown mosquito with pale bands on the proboscis and legs. Spreads Japanese encephalitis, Murray Valley encephalitis and Ross River virus.

species.name: Apis mellifera
species.note: Brown and black bee with a hairy thorax. Stings cause more deaths in Australia than snakebite, through anaphylaxis in allergic people.

species.name: Synanceia verrucosa
species.note: Warty, mottled fish that looks like a rock or coral. Thirteen dorsal spines inject venom when stepped on. Pain is extreme; antivenom exists and no Australian deaths are confirmed.

species.name: Synanceia horrida
species.note: Lumpy, mud-coloured stonefish of estuaries and seagrass. Wear shoes on tidal flats.

species.name: Notesthes robusta
species.note: Mottled brown freshwater scorpionfish with venomous dorsal spines. Lurks in rivers and creeks of eastern Queensland.

species.name: Pterois volitans
species.note: Red and white stripes with long, feathery venomous fin spines. Painful sting; not usually dangerous to life.

species.name: Plotosus lineatus
species.note: Eel-like catfish with white stripes and whiskers; often in tight schools. Venomous fin spines cause severe pain.

species.name: Bathytoshia brevicaudata
species.note: Very large grey ray with a serrated barb on the tail. Wounds are painful and can be deep; a chest strike off Batt Reef killed Steve Irwin in 2006, but deaths are rare.

species.name: Physalia utriculus
species.note: Blue gas-filled float with a single long blue tentacle. The most common sting in Queensland. Painful but rarely serious.

species.name: Morbakka fenneri
species.note: Box jelly with a tall, see-through bell and four tentacles. Can cause Irukandji-like symptoms. Found further south than most stingers, including Moreton Bay.

species.name: Acanthaster solaris
species.note: Large starfish with many arms covered in long venomous spines. Painful, slow-healing wounds. Eats coral on the Great Barrier Reef.

species.name: Toxopneustes pileolus
species.note: Short-spined urchin covered in pink or white flower-like pincers that inject venom. Do not handle.

species.name: Millepora platyphylla
species.note: Mustard-yellow coral with white tips. Not a true coral; tiny stinging cells cause burning welts.

species.name: Latrodectus hasselti
species.note: Black spider with a red stripe on the abdomen. Bites cause severe pain and sweating. Deaths stopped after antivenom arrived in 1956.

species.name: Missulena bradleyi
species.note: Stocky, shiny black spider; males have a blue abdomen. Bites are rare but can be serious.

species.name: Ixodes holocyclus
species.note: Small grey tick with dark legs, especially the front pair. Can cause paralysis, severe allergy and red-meat allergy.

species.name: Myrmecia gulosa
species.note: Large ant with a red head and thorax, long jaws and a powerful sting. Anaphylaxis is possible.

species.name: Ethmostigmus rubripes
species.note: Long, flattened centipede, often orange or blue-green with yellow legs. The bite is extremely painful.

species.name: Ochrogaster lunifer
species.note: Hairy caterpillars that travel nose-to-tail in processions. Their hairs cause rashes and eye injuries.

species.name: Ornithorhynchus anatinus
species.note: Duck-billed, furry swimmer. Males have a venomous spur on each hind leg; the pain can last for weeks.

species.name: Rhinella marina
species.note: Warty brown toad with large swollen glands behind the head. Toxin can harm human eyes and kills pet dogs. Introduced.

species.name: Crocodylus johnstoni
species.note: Long, narrow snout and a row of large scales behind the head. Bites if disturbed but does not hunt people.

species.name: Sus scrofa
species.note: Bristly black or brown pig; boars have curved tusks. Charges when cornered. Introduced.

species.name: Macropus giganteus
species.note: Large grey kangaroo. Big males kick and claw when they feel threatened, especially in suburbs and golf courses.

species.name: Dromaius novaehollandiae
species.note: Tall shaggy brown bird. Kicks forward with powerful, clawed feet.

species.name: Gymnorhina tibicen
species.note: Black and white songbird. A few males swoop people in spring and can injure eyes.

species.name: Varanus varius
species.note: Large dark goanna with pale bands and spots. Sharp claws and a bite that often becomes infected.

species.name: Orectolobus maculatus
species.note: Flat, carpet-patterned shark with a beard of skin flaps. Bites and holds on when stepped on or grabbed.

species.name: Gymnothorax javanicus
species.note: Huge brown moray covered in dark spots. Bites hard when hands go into its crevice.

species.name: Aurelia aurita
species.note: Flat, saucer-shaped bell with four pale horseshoe rings and short fringe tentacles. Sting is too weak to notice.

species.name: Catostylus mosaicus
species.note: Firm, dome-shaped bell, blue to brown, with frilly arms and no long tentacles. Mild sting at most.

species.name: Cassiopea andromeda
species.note: Lies upside down on mangrove and seagrass mud with its frilly arms facing up. Very mild sting.

species.name: Velella velella
species.note: Small blue oval float with a stiff clear sail. Washes up with bluebottles but is harmless.

species.name: Porpita porpita
species.note: Flat blue disc with a fringe of short blue tentacles. Can irritate sensitive skin but is not dangerous.

species.name: Octopus cyanea
species.note: Medium octopus that changes colour and texture fast; no blue rings. Hunts on reef flats by day.

species.name: Cypraea tigris
species.note: Glossy, egg-shaped shell with black spots. Harmless, unlike cone shells.

species.name: Hemiscyllium ocellatum
species.note: Small, slim bottom shark with a big black spot ringed in white above each pectoral fin. Walks on its fins across reef flats.

species.name: Stegostoma tigrinum
species.note: Adults are pale with dark spots, a long tail and ridges along the body. Docile reef shark.

species.name: Carcharias taurus
species.note: Bulky shark with ragged teeth that show at all times. Looks fierce but is placid.

species.name: Rhincodon typus
species.note: The largest fish; checkerboard of white spots and stripes. Filter feeder.

species.name: Mobula alfredi
species.note: Huge diamond-shaped ray with head fins and no tail barb. Gentle plankton feeder.

species.name: Dugong dugon
species.note: Grey sea mammal with a fluked tail and a broad downturned snout. Grazes on seagrass.

species.name: Heteropoda jugulans
species.note: Large, flat, leggy brown spider found on walls and in cars. Scary but harmless; the bite may hurt.

species.name: Tasmanicosa godeffroyi
species.note: Hairy brown ground spider with a radiating pattern on the back. Not dangerous.

species.name: Trichonephila plumipes
species.note: Long-legged spider with feathery leg tufts and a golden web. Harmless.

species.name: Lampona cylindrata
species.note: Slim, dark grey spider with a white tail tip. Claims that its bite causes ulcers are a myth.

species.name: Vanellus miles
species.note: Plover with a yellow face mask and wing spurs. Swoops loudly near nests but almost never strikes.

species.name: Burhinus grallarius
species.note: Tall grey bird with big yellow eyes. Its wailing night call sounds alarming, but it is harmless.

species.name: Tiliqua scincoides
species.note: Stout, banded skink that hisses and flashes a blue tongue. Harmless.

species.name: Chlamydosaurus kingii
species.note: Spreads a huge neck frill and gapes when threatened. All show.

species.name: Intellagama lesueurii
species.note: Big dragon with a dark band behind the eye, common around creeks and parks. Harmless.

species.name: Tachyglossus aculeatus
species.note: Spiny ant-eating monotreme. Unlike the platypus, it has no venom.

species.name: Trichosurus vulpecula
species.note: Grey possum with a bushy black tail and pointed ears. Noisy in roofs, harmless.

species.name: Lates calcarifer
species.note: Silver fish with a concave forehead and large mouth. Prized table fish, harmless.

species.name: Epinephelus lanceolatus
species.note: Massive, mottled grouper of reefs and jetties. Curious and harmless.

species.name: Litoria caerulea
species.note: Plump, bright green frog with sticky toe pads, often in bathrooms and downpipes. Harmless.

species.name: Limnodynastes tasmaniensis
species.note: Small frog with dark olive spots and a pale back stripe. Often confused with young cane toads.
